You have an Azure subscription linked to an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named `contoso.onmicrosoft.com`. The subscription contains these resources:  
  
- A virtual network named `Vnet1`  
- An App Service plan named `ASP1`  
- An Azure App Service named `webapp1`  
- An Azure private DNS zone named `private.contoso.com`  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783812716261-2ysaabfh.png)  
  
- Virtual machines on `Vnet1` that cannot communicate outside the virtual network  
  
You need to ensure that the virtual machines on `Vnet1` can access `webapp1` by using the URL `https://www.private.contoso.com`.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer is part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Create a CNAME record that maps www.private.contoso.com to webapp1.contoso.onmicrosoft.com.
Create a CNAME record that maps www.private.contoso.com to webapp1.private.contoso.com.
Create a service endpoint for webapp1.
Register an enterprise application in Azure AD for webapp1.
Create a private endpoint for webapp1.
Create a CNAME record that maps www.private.contoso.com to webapp1.privatelink.azurewebsites.net.

questions.explanation:
An App Service private endpoint assigns private network access to the app from the virtual network. A CNAME for `www.private.contoso.com` that targets `webapp1.privatelink.azurewebsites.net` directs the custom hostname to the App Service Private Link endpoint, allowing the virtual machines to reach the app without Internet connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Use Private Endpoints for Apps - Azure App Service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/overview-private-endpoint) · [Azure Private Endpoint private DNS zone values](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/private-link/private-endpoint-dns)

You create a virtual network named Vnet2 in the West US region.  
  
You plan to enable peering between Vnet1 and Vnet2.  
  
You need to ensure that virtual machines connected to Vnet2 can connect to VM1 and VM2 through LB1.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: From the Peerings settings of Vnet2, set Traffic forwarded from remote virtual network to Allow.
Change the Floating IP configurations of LB1.
From the Peerings settings of Vnet1, set Traffic forwarded from remote virtual network to Allow.

questions.explanation:
Global virtual network peering connects virtual networks in different Azure regions. Resources in a globally peered virtual network cannot reach back-end resources through the front-end IP address of a Basic Load Balancer. This restriction does not apply to a Standard Load Balancer, so LB1 must use the Standard SKU.

**Learn more:** [Azure Virtual Network FAQ](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-za/azure/virtual-network/virtual-networks-faq) · [Troubleshoot virtual network peering issues](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-troubleshoot-peering-issues)

An Azure subscription contains a virtual machine named VM1 and a network security group (NSG) named NSG1. NSG1 has its default rules configured. VM1 runs Windows Server 2022 and has one NIC, named NIC1. NIC1 is associated with NSG1.  
  
You need to block access to the Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) REST API from VM1. The solution must minimize administrative effort.  
  
What should you add to NSG1?

options.text: an outbound rule that blocks traffic to an IP address.
an inbound rule that blocks traffic to an IP address.
an inbound and outbound rule that blocks traffic to an application security group.
an outbound rule that blocks traffic to a service tag.

questions.explanation:
Azure IMDS is available to a VM at the link-local address `169.254.169.254`; access to it originates from the VM and is therefore outbound traffic. A higher-priority outbound deny rule for that destination IP overrides the default outbound allow rules and blocks IMDS access.

**Learn more:** [Azure Instance Metadata Service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/instance-metadata-service) · [How network security groups filter network traffic](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/network-security-group-how-it-works)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You purchase an Azure subscription and plan to deploy the resources shown in the following table to that subscription.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784206592284-s9zxj1ax.png)  
  
You need to create an NSG1 rule named Rule1 that meets these requirements:  
  
- Allow the search servers of App1 to establish outbound HTTP connections to internet services.  
- Minimize administrative effort when new search servers are deployed.  
- Apply the principle of least privilege.  
  
What should you choose as the source for Rule1?
questions.explanation:
An application security group can group the network interfaces of App1’s search servers by workload role and be used as the source in an NSG rule. Adding newly deployed search servers to that group automatically includes them in the rule, while restricting the outbound HTTP allowance to those servers rather than the entire subnet or virtual network.

**Learn more:** [Network security groups and application security groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/design-guide/network-application-security-groups)

questions.domain: Design and implement application delivery services
questions.question:
Solution: Disable the WAF rule with ruleId **920300**.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
Rule 920300 is the Azure WAF protocol-enforcement rule for a request missing an `Accept` header. Disabling it prevents that rule from blocking the request, so the URL can be accessed through the application gateway.\
\
**Learn more:** [CRS and DRS rule groups and rules - Azure Web Application Firewall](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/web-application-firewall/ag/application-gateway-crs-rulegroups-rules?tabs=owasp31) · [Troubleshoot WAF blocking legitimate requests (HTTP 403 Forbidden errors) in Azure Application Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/application-gateway/troubleshoot-waf-blocking-legitimate-requests-403)

You are designing the IP address space for subnets in Azure virtual networks.  
  
Which resource type needs IP addresses within the subnets?

options.text: Azure DDoS Protection for virtual networks

questions.explanation:
An internal load balancer uses a private frontend IP address from the selected virtual-network subnet; therefore, its frontend configuration consumes a subnet IP address. Service endpoints, service endpoint policies, and Azure DDoS Protection do not require their own subnet IP addresses.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer portal settings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/manage) · [Azure Load Balancer components](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/components)

questions.domain: Design and implement private access to Azure services
questions.question:
You are designing the IP address space for subnets in Azure virtual networks.  
  
Which resource type needs IP addresses within the subnets?
questions.explanation:
An application security group logically groups the network interfaces of the monitoring virtual machines and can be used as the destination of an NSG rule. Membership can be assigned to each new monitoring VM without modifying the NSG rule, while other virtual machines in the same subnets remain outside the allowed destination group.

**Learn more:** [Network security groups and application security groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/design-guide/network-application-security-groups) · [Azure Application Security Groups Overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/application-security-groups)

You create a service endpoint policy with these settings:  
  
- Associated subnets: Subnet1  
- Service: Microsoft.Storage  
- Scope: Single account  
- Resource: storage1  
  
Which resources can VM1 access?

options.text: storage1 in the East US Azure region and its replica in the paired region
storage1 in the East US Azure region only
storage1 and storage2 in the East US Azure region only
storage1 and storage2 in the East US Azure region and their replicas in the paired region

questions.explanation:
A service endpoint policy allowlists the specified Azure Storage account for traffic over the service endpoint from the associated subnet. Because only storage1 is listed, storage2 is denied. When an RA-GRS primary storage account is listed in a service endpoint policy, access to its read-access secondary replica is automatically allowed.

**Learn more:** [Azure virtual network service endpoint policies overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/id-id/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-service-endpoint-policies-overview) · [Create and associate service endpoint policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-service-endpoint-policies)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are planning an Azure deployment that will include three virtual networks in the East US Azure region, as shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783826682804-5b5c5yk1.png)  
  
A Site-to-Site VPN will connect Vnet1 to your company's on-premises network.  
  
You need to recommend a solution that ensures the virtual machines on every virtual network can communicate with the on-premises network. The solution must minimize costs.  
  
What should you recommend for Vnet2 and Vnet3?
questions.explanation:
Virtual network peering with gateway transit lets Vnet2 and Vnet3 use the VPN gateway in Vnet1 for connectivity to the on-premises network. Sharing the existing gateway avoids the cost of separate VPN gateways or VNet-to-VNet VPN connections.

**Learn more:** [Azure Virtual Network peering overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-peering-overview) · [Configure VPN gateway transit for virtual network peering](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/vpn-gateway-peering-gateway-transit)

questions.question:
You intend to configure BGP for a Site-to-Site VPN connection between a datacenter and Azure.  
  
Which two Azure resources must you configure? Each correct answer represents part of the solution. (Choose two.)  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
A Site-to-Site VPN with BGP uses a virtual network gateway as the Azure VPN gateway and a local network gateway to represent the on-premises VPN device. BGP settings on these resources provide the Azure and on-premises BGP peer information needed for dynamic route exchange.\
\
**Learn more:** [How to configure BGP for Azure VPN Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/bgp-howto) · [Azure VPN Gateway configuration settings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/vpn-gateway-about-vpn-gateway-settings)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription containing the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784206597472-9b31jxm3.png)  
  
NSG1 is linked to the NIC for VM1 and includes the rules shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784206601462-q8kei443.png)  
  
You collect NSG flow logs for five minutes for these activities:  
  
- Two RDP sessions from VM1 to VM2, each started from a different TCP port  
- Three SSH sessions from VM2 to VM1, each started from a different TCP port  
  
You analyze the logs by using Traffic Analytics in Azure Network Watcher.  
  
How many aggregated flow entries will Traffic Analytics identify?
questions.explanation:
Traffic Analytics aggregates NSG flows that share the source and destination IP addresses, destination port, NSG and rule, direction, and transport protocol. It excludes the source port from the aggregation key. Thus, the two RDP sessions aggregate into one outbound RDP entry and the three SSH sessions aggregate into one inbound SSH entry, for two entries in total.

**Learn more:** [Traffic analytics schema and data aggregation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/traffic-analytics-schema) · [Traffic analytics overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/traffic-analytics)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to deploy an Azure virtual network containing 10 virtual subnets. The subnets will use IPv6 addresses. Each subnet will host up to 200 load-balanced virtual machines.  
  
You need to recommend a load-balancing solution for the virtual network. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- The virtual machines and the load balancer must be accessible only from within the virtual network.  
- Costs must be minimized.  
  
What should you include in the recommendation?
questions.explanation:
An internal Azure Standard Load Balancer provides a private frontend that is accessible within the virtual network and supports IPv6. It supports up to 5,000 backend-pool instances, accommodating the potential 2,000 virtual machines across the 10 subnets. Basic Load Balancer supports only 300 backend IP configurations and has been retired.

**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer SKUs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/skus) · [Azure subscription and service limits, quotas, and constraints](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/management/azure-subscription-service-limits)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have two Azure virtual networks in the East US Azure region, as shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783831418810-9j9o88q3.png)  
  
The virtual networks are peered with each other. Each virtual network has four subnets.  
  
You plan to deploy a virtual machine named VM1 to inspect and route traffic among all subnets across both virtual networks.  
  
What is the minimum number of IP addresses that you must assign to VM1?
questions.explanation:
A single private IP address on VM1 can be used as the next hop for user-defined routes. Azure virtual network peering supports service chaining, which permits routes to point to a virtual appliance VM in a peered virtual network. With IP forwarding and the required route and peering configuration, that one appliance interface can inspect and forward traffic among the subnets in both virtual networks.

**Learn more:** [Azure Virtual Network Peering](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-peering-overview) · [Route network traffic with a route table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/tutorial-create-route-table)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription containing the Azure App Service web apps shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783831428478-dmk76wji.png)  
  
You need to deploy Azure Traffic Manager. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Traffic for `https://www.fabrikam.com` must be directed to App1eu.  
- If App1eu becomes unresponsive, all traffic for `https://www.fabrikam.com` must be directed to App1us.  
  
You need to implement Traffic Manager to meet the requirements.  
  
Which two resources should you create? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: a Traffic Manager profile that uses the priority routing method
a Traffic Manager profile that uses the geographic routing method
a CNAME record in a DNS domain named fabrikam.com
a TXT record in a DNS domain named fabricam.com
a real user measurements key in Traffic Manager

questions.explanation:
Traffic Manager Priority routing designates a primary endpoint and uses lower-priority endpoints as backups; it routes traffic to the backup when health monitoring determines the primary is unavailable. To route the custom hostname `www.fabrikam.com` through the Traffic Manager profile, the DNS zone for `fabrikam.com` needs a CNAME record mapping that hostname to the profile’s `trafficmanager.net` name.

**Learn more:** [Traffic Manager routing methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/traffic-manager/traffic-manager-routing-methods) · [Point a company Internet domain to an Azure Traffic Manager domain](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/traffic-manager/traffic-manager-point-internet-domain)

You plan to migrate the website to an Azure web app named `Web1`. The website on `Web1` will be published by using an Azure Front Door instance named `ContosoFD1`.  
  
You build the website on `Web1`.  
  
You plan to configure `ContosoFD1` to publish the website for testing.  
  
When you try to configure a custom domain for `www.contoso.com` on `ContosoFD1`, you receive the error message shown in the exhibit. (Click the Exhibit tab.)  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783807252917-pw27qjsy.jpg)  
  
You need to test the website and `ContosoFD1` without affecting user access to the on-premises web server.  
  
Which record should you create in the `contoso.com` DNS domain?

options.text: a CNAME record that maps afdverify.www.contoso.com to ContosoFD1.azurefd.net
a CNAME record that maps www.contoso.com to ContosoFD1.azurefd.net
a CNAME record that maps afdverify.www.contoso.com to afdverify.ContosoFD1.azurefd.net
a CNAME record that maps www.contoso.com to Web1.contoso.com

questions.explanation:
Azure Front Door supports a temporary `afdverify` CNAME to validate a production custom domain without changing the production `www` DNS mapping. The validation record must map `afdverify.www.contoso.com` to `afdverify.ContosoFD1.azurefd.net`; the existing `www.contoso.com` record continues to route users to the on-premises server. You are planning an Azure Point-to-Site (P2S) VPN that uses OpenVPN.  
  
Users will authenticate through an on-premises Active Directory domain.  
  
Which additional service must you deploy to support VPN authentication?

options.text: Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Application Proxy

questions.explanation:
Azure P2S VPN authentication against an on-premises Active Directory domain requires a RADIUS server that integrates with Active Directory. OpenVPN supports RADIUS authentication for P2S connections.\
\
**Learn more:** [About Azure Point-to-Site VPN connections - Azure VPN Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/point-to-site-about) · [Configure VPN gateway for P2S RADIUS authentication - Azure VPN Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/point-to-site-radius-gateway)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to manage connectivity from NYCNet to Azure services that use private endpoints. The solution must satisfy the security requirements.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: From Azure Virtual Network Manager, create a security admin configuration.
From Azure Virtual Network Manager, create a network group that has Member type set to Subnet.
Add a route table to SUBNET-PE.
Enable a network policy for SUBNET-PE.

questions.explanation:
Private-endpoint network policies are disabled by default on a subnet. Enable the network policy for `SUBNET-PE` before using a route table to control traffic to private endpoints; this permits user-defined routes to be evaluated for private-endpoint traffic and supports blocking access from NYCNet while preserving required access from Azure virtual machines. [Manage network policies for private endpoints](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/private-link/disable-private-endpoint-network-policy)

You need to configure APPGW1 to enable end-to-end encryption. The solution must satisfy the security requirements.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: From the SSL settings, upload a TLS client certificate that is issued by the internal root CA and includes the full certificate chain.
From the Backend settings, upload the internal root CA certificate.
From the SSL settings, upload a TLS client certificate that is issued by the internal root CA.
From the Backend settings, upload a wildcard TLS certificate that has a private key issued by the internal root CA.

questions.explanation:
Application Gateway WAF v2 requires a trusted root certificate for backend TLS when backend certificates are issued by a private CA. Uploading the internal root CA certificate in Backend settings enables Application Gateway to validate the HTTPS certificate presented by the backend servers, preserving encryption from the client through to the backend.

**Learn more:** [Azure Application Gateway Backend Settings configuration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/configuration-http-settings) · [Certificates required to allow backend servers - Azure Application Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/certificates-for-backend-authentication)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to configure FD1 to provide users with access to app2.proseware.com. The solution must satisfy the security requirements and the general requirements.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: Request a certificate from a trusted root CA.
Add a security policy to FD1.
Add a custom domain to FD1.
Export the TLS certificate and the private key from App2.

questions.explanation:
Azure Front Door Standard must have `app2.proseware.com` configured as a validated custom domain before the domain can be associated with a Front Door endpoint and route, enabling traffic for that hostname to flow through FD1. HTTPS/TLS configuration is applied to the custom domain, and a WAF security policy can only be associated with domains that have already been added.

**Learn more:** [Add a custom domain to Azure Front Door](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/frontdoor/standard-premium/how-to-add-custom-domain) · [Configure HTTPS for a custom domain in Azure Front Door](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/frontdoor/standard-premium/how-to-configure-https-custom-domain)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to configure a custom rule for APPGW1-WAFPolicy that allows only connections originating from FD1. The solution must support the planned changes.  
  
Which **Match type** and **Match variable** should you select?
questions.explanation:
Azure Front Door adds the `X-Azure-FDID` request header containing the unique identifier of the Front Door profile when it sends a request to an origin. An Application Gateway WAF custom rule should validate this header’s expected FD1 value, using a string match on `RequestHeaders`, to restrict APPGW1 access to FD1. IP-based filtering alone cannot distinguish the specific Front Door profile because Azure Front Door backend IP addresses can be shared and change.

**Learn more:** [Secure traffic to origins - Azure Front Door](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/frontdoor/origin-security) · [Create and use WAF v2 custom rules on Application Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/web-application-firewall/ag/create-custom-waf-rules)

questions.question:
You need to create a security rule for APPGW1-NSG1. The solution must support the planned changes.  
  
Which service tag should you use?
questions.explanation:
APPGW1 is FD1’s origin, so its NSG must allow the inbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic that Azure Front Door sends to an origin. The `AzureFrontDoor.Backend` service tag contains the Azure Front Door addresses used to access origins and is the tag used to secure an Application Gateway origin behind Front Door.\
\
**Learn more:** [Secure traffic to Azure Front Door origins](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/frontdoor/origin-security) · [Azure service tags overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/service-tags-overview)

questions.question:
You must configure the default route on Vnet2 and Vnet3. The solution must satisfy the virtual networking requirements.  
  
What should you use to configure the default route?

options.text: a user-defined route assigned to GatewaySubnet in Vnet1
a user-defined route assigned to GatewaySubnet in Vnet2 and Vnet3

questions.explanation:
BGP route exchange can advertise a `0.0.0.0/0` default route through an Azure virtual network gateway. Azure adds BGP-advertised routes to the route tables of subnets in the virtual network. A `0.0.0.0/0` user-defined route on `GatewaySubnet` is not supported.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure virtual network traffic routing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-networks-udr-overview) · [Azure VPN Gateway configuration settings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/vpn-gateway-about-vpn-gateway-settings)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an on-premises server named Server1 with the IP address `10.1.1.1`, which hosts a DNS zone named `contoso.com`.  
  
You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783925271775-njv9tf0x.png)  
  
You discover that VM1 cannot resolve the DNS name of PEP1.  
  
You need to ensure that VM1 can resolve the DNS names for the private endpoints. The solution must minimize administrative effort.  
  
What should you configure on Server1?
questions.explanation:
Because VM1 is configured to use Server1 as its DNS server, Server1 must forward private-endpoint DNS queries to the Azure DNS resolution path that can resolve the private DNS zone associated with the endpoint. A conditional forwarder targets only the applicable private DNS namespace and avoids manually creating and maintaining DNS records. Microsoft recommends configuring an on-premises DNS solution with a conditional forwarder for the private DNS zone when resolving private endpoint names.

**Learn more:** [Azure Private Endpoint DNS Integration Scenarios](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/private-link/private-endpoint-dns-integration)

You manage an Azure Virtual Desktop environment consisting of 500 session hosts. All outbound internet traffic from these hosts is routed through a NAT gateway.  
  
During peak business hours, some users report they are unable to reach resources on the internet. Using Azure Monitor, you find a large number of failed SNAT connections.  
  
You need to increase the number of available SNAT connections.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Bind the NAT gateway to another subnet.
Deploy Azure Standard Load Balancer that has outbound rules.

questions.explanation:
Azure NAT Gateway allocates 64,512 SNAT ports per public IP address attached to it, and supports up to 16 public IPs (or an equivalent public IP prefix), for a maximum of roughly 1,032,192 SNAT ports. When session hosts hit SNAT exhaustion under load, Microsoft's documented scaling guidance is to associate additional public IP addresses (or a public IP prefix) with the NAT gateway to increase the pool of available outbound SNAT ports. Associating the NAT gateway with an additional subnet does not add SNAT capacity—it just lets more resources draw from the same limited pool, worsening exhaustion. A Standard Load Balancer with outbound rules is irrelevant here because when a subnet is associated with a NAT gateway, the NAT gateway takes precedence for all outbound flows and Load Balancer outbound SNAT rules are bypassed.

**Learn more:** [Source Network Address Translation (SNAT) with Azure NAT Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/nat-gateway/nat-gateway-snat) · [Manage a public IP address with a NAT gateway - Azure Virtual Network](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/ip-services/configure-public-ip-nat-gateway)

You test DDoSplan1 by running a simulation that targets IP1.  
  
You need to review the DDoS Protection mitigation reports.  
  
What should you use?

options.text: DDos protection plan in the Azure portal

questions.explanation:
Azure DDoS Protection mitigation reports are emitted as the DDoSMitigationReports diagnostic-log category. To review them you route the resource's diagnostic logs to a Log Analytics workspace and query them (for example, AzureDiagnostics | where Category == 'DDoSMitigationReports'). Microsoft's dedicated procedure is titled 'View Azure DDoS Protection logs in a Log Analytics workspace', so the tool to use is Log Analytics (B). The DDoS Protection plan blade surfaces near-real-time metrics rather than the detailed mitigation reports, and neither Defender for Cloud nor Network Insights is where these reports are reviewed.

**Learn more:** [View Azure DDoS Protection logs in Log Analytics workspace](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ddos-protection/ddos-view-diagnostic-logs)

You plan to deploy an Azure Virtual Network NAT gateway named Gateway1. The solution must satisfy these requirements:  
  
- VM1 will access the internet by using its public IP address.  
- VM2 will access the internet by using its public IP address.  
- Administrative effort must be minimized.  
  
You need to ensure that Gateway1 can be deployed to Vnet1.  
  
What is the minimum number of subnets required in Vnet1?
questions.explanation:
A NAT gateway cannot be deployed to a gateway subnet, and a subnet associated with a NAT gateway cannot contain Basic SKU resources such as VM1's Basic SKU public IP. In addition, a NAT gateway takes precedence over an instance-level public IP for outbound connections, so associating it with the VM subnet would prevent VM2 from using its own public IP for internet egress. Vnet1 therefore needs its existing VM subnet and GatewaySubnet, plus a separate subnet for the NAT gateway.

**Learn more:** [What is Azure NAT Gateway?](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/nat-gateway/nat-overview) · [Troubleshoot Azure NAT Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/nat-gateway/troubleshoot-nat)

Each virtual network includes 20 internet-accessible resources that have public IP addresses assigned.  
  
You need to deploy Azure DDoS Network Protection to protect the resources. The solution must minimize costs.  
  
What is the minimum number of DDoS Network Protection plans that you should deploy?
questions.explanation:
A single Azure DDoS Network Protection plan can be associated with virtual networks in multiple subscriptions and regions when the subscriptions belong to the same Microsoft Entra tenant. One plan covers all four virtual networks in the contoso.com tenant, while a second plan is required for the virtual networks in the separate fabrikam.com tenant. Each plan covers fewer than 100 protected public IP addresses.

**Learn more:** [Azure DDoS Protection overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ddos-protection/ddos-protection-overview) · [Manage DDoS Protection plans: permissions and restrictions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ddos-protection/manage-permissions)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription containing the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784206598510-pymgap1l.png)  
  
You need to ensure that the virtual machines can access storage1, storage2, and DB1 by using service endpoints.  
  
What is the minimum number of service endpoints that you should create?
questions.explanation:
Azure Storage accounts share the Microsoft.Storage endpoint type, so storage1 and storage2 do not require separate endpoint types. Azure SQL Database uses Microsoft.Sql. Service endpoints are configured for subnets in the VNet and are not transitive across VNet peering, so both endpoint types are required in VNet1 and VNet2, for a minimum of four service endpoint configurations.

**Learn more:** [Azure virtual network service endpoints](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-service-endpoints-overview) · [Available Endpoint Services - List](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/virtualnetwork/available-endpoint-services/list?view=rest-virtualnetwork-2025-05-01)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure virtual network containing the subnets shown in the exhibit:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784174072197-jppjon0h.png)  
  
You deploy an Azure Firewall to the AzureFirewallSubnet. You configure routing so that all traffic from Subnet2 passes through the firewall.  
  
You need to ensure that all hosts on Subnet2 can reach an external site at https://*.contoso.com.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: In a firewall policy, create a DNAT rule.
Create a network security group (NSG) and associate the NSG to Subnet2.
In a firewall policy, create a network rule.
In a firewall policy, create an application rule.

questions.explanation:
Azure Firewall application rules control outbound access based on fully qualified domain names (FQDNs), including wildcard patterns like *.contoso.com, for HTTP/HTTPS traffic. Since the goal is to permit Subnet2 hosts to reach a specific external domain over HTTPS, you must define an application rule in the firewall policy that allows traffic to that FQDN. Network rules filter by IP address, port, and protocol rather than domain name, DNAT rules handle inbound traffic translation (not outbound access), and NSGs don't provide FQDN-based application filtering integrated with Azure Firewall policies.

**Learn more:** [Azure Firewall application rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/rule-processing#application-rules) · [Deploy and configure Azure Firewall - application rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/tutorial-firewall-deploy-portal)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that includes the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783918541794-o4per3mu.png)  
  
You need to manage access to storage1 by using NSG1.  
  
What should you configure first?
questions.explanation:
A private endpoint is deployed in Subnet1 and NSG1 is linked to that subnet. Private endpoint network policies are disabled by default on a subnet; enabling the policy is required before network security group rules can control traffic to the private endpoint that accesses storage1.

**Learn more:** [Manage network policies for private endpoints - Azure Private Link](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/private-link/disable-private-endpoint-network-policy) · [What is a private endpoint? - Azure Private Link](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/private-link/private-endpoint-overview)

You have an on-premises DNS server named Server that hosts a primary DNS zone named fabrikam.com.  
  
You have an Azure subscription containing the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784206596522-zqamozx2.png)  
  
Users on the on-premises network access resources on all the virtual networks by using a Site-to-Site (S2S) VPN.  
  
You need to deploy an Azure DNS Private Resolver solution that meets these requirements:  
  
- Resources connected to the virtual networks must be able to resolve DNS names for fabrikam.com.  
- Server1 must be able to resolve the DNS names of the resources in contoso.com.  
- The solution must minimize costs and administrative effort.  
  
What is the minimum number of resolvers that you should deploy?
questions.explanation:
Azure DNS Private Resolver uses outbound endpoints and forwarding rulesets to conditionally forward Azure DNS queries to on-premises DNS servers, while inbound endpoints allow on-premises DNS servers to resolve records in a private DNS zone. A resolver can reference only a virtual network in the same region, and a forwarding ruleset cannot be linked to a VNet in another region. Separate resolvers are therefore required for West US and West Europe; an inbound endpoint in the VNet linked to contoso.com enables Server1 to resolve that private zone.

**Learn more:** [Azure DNS Private Resolver overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/dns/dns-private-resolver-overview) · [Azure DNS Private Resolver endpoints and rulesets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/dns/private-resolver-endpoints-rulesets)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an on-premises server named Server1 that runs Windows Server.  
  
You have an Azure subscription containing a virtual network named VNet1.  
  
You plan to connect Server1 to VNet1 by using Azure Network Adapter.  
  
You need to minimize the time required to deploy the adapter to Server1.  
  
What should you create first?
questions.explanation:
Azure Network Adapter connects a server to an Azure virtual network through a point-to-site VPN connection. It needs an Azure virtual network gateway; if no gateway exists, Windows Admin Center creates one during adapter setup, which can take up to 25 minutes. Precreating the Azure VPN gateway minimizes adapter deployment time.

**Learn more:** [Use Azure Network Adapter to connect a server to an Azure Virtual Network](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/manage/windows-admin-center/azure/use-azure-network-adapter)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) instance on Azure Front Door.  
  
You plan to create a WAF rule that blocks high request rates originating from a single IP address.  
  
You need to query Log Analytics to determine the optimal threshold for the rule.  
  
Which Log Analytics table should you query?
questions.explanation:
Azure Front Door logs, including Front Door access and WAF log categories, are stored in the `AzureDiagnostics` table when routed to Log Analytics. That table contains client IP and request data that can be aggregated to establish an appropriate per-IP rate-limit threshold.

**Learn more:** [Monitoring data reference for Azure Front Door](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/frontdoor/monitor-front-door-reference) · [Example log table queries for AzureDiagnostics](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/reference/queries/azurediagnostics)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure virtual machine named VM1.  
  
You need to capture all network traffic from VM1 by using Azure Network Watcher.  
  
To which locations can the capture be saved?

options.text: a file path on VM1 only
a Block blob premium account only
General purpose v2 standard and a file path on VM1 only
General purpose v2 standard and a Block blob premium account only
blob storage, a file path on VM1, and a Block blob premium account

questions.explanation:
Azure Network Watcher packet captures can be saved to Azure Blob Storage, to a local file on the target virtual machine, or to both destinations. A standard general-purpose v2 storage account is supported, whereas premium storage accounts are not supported for storing packet captures.

**Learn more:** [Manage Packet Captures - Azure Network Watcher](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/packet-capture-manage) · [Packet Capture Overview - Azure Network Watcher](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/packet-capture-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription containing these resources:  
  
- A virtual network named Vnet1  
- Two subnets named subnet1 and AzureFirewallSubnet  
- A public Azure Firewall named FW1  
- A route table named RT1 associated with subnet1  
- A rule in RT1 that routes `0.0.0.0/0` to FW1  
  
After deploying 10 servers running Windows Server to subnet1, you find that none of the virtual machines are activated.  
  
You need to make sure that the virtual machines can be activated.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: On FW1, configure a DNAT rule for port 1688.
Deploy an application security group that allows outbound traffic to 1688.
On FW1, create an outbound network rule that allows traffic to the Azure Key Management Service (KMS).
On FW1, create an outbound service tag rule for Azure Cloud.

questions.explanation:
Azure Windows VMs activate through the Azure Key Management Service (KMS) endpoint. Because the default route sends their outbound traffic through Azure Firewall, the firewall needs an outbound network rule that permits KMS connectivity on TCP port 1688. Microsoft documents `azkms.core.windows.net:1688` as the Azure public-cloud KMS endpoint and specifies allowing outbound access to KMS through the firewall.

**Learn more:** [Windows VM activation no longer works in Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-machines/windows/windows-activation-stopped-working) · [Troubleshoot Windows virtual machine activation problems in Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-machines/windows/troubleshoot-activation-problems)

You need to ensure that apps hosted on VM1 can resolve the private endpoint IP address for azsql1.database.windows.net.  
  
What should you create first?

options.text: a public DNS zone named database.windows.net
a private DNS zone named database.windows.net
a public DNS zone named privatelink.database.windows.net
a private DNS zone named privatelink.database.windows.net

questions.explanation:
For Azure SQL Database private endpoints, the recommended private DNS zone is `privatelink.database.windows.net`. A private DNS zone can contain the private endpoint’s A record and be linked to VNet1, allowing workloads on VM1 to resolve the SQL server name to the private IP address.

**Learn more:** [Azure Private Endpoint private DNS zone values](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/private-link/private-endpoint-dns) · [Azure Private Endpoint DNS integration scenarios](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/private-link/private-endpoint-dns-integration)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription containing the resources shown in the following table.

Users on HP1 access App1 by using the URL `https://app1.contoso.com`.  
  
You need to ensure that the IDPS on FW1 can detect security threats in connections from HP1 to Server1.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer provides part of the solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Import a server certificate to KV1.
Add an application group to HP1.
Add a secured virtual network to FW1.

questions.explanation:
Azure Firewall Premium cannot inspect the contents of HTTPS traffic unless TLS inspection is enabled. TLS inspection decrypts the connection so the IDPS can evaluate it for threats, and its configuration requires a valid intermediate CA certificate to be stored in Azure Key Vault.

**Learn more:** [Azure Firewall Premium certificates](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/premium-certificates) · [Azure Firewall Premium features implementation guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/premium-features)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription containing the resources shown in the following table.

You plan to deploy an Azure Virtual Network NAT gateway named Gateway1. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- VM1 must access the internet by using its public IP address.  
- VM2 must access the internet by using its public IP address.  
- Administrative effort must be minimized.  
  
You need to ensure that Gateway1 can be deployed to Vnet1.  
  
What is the minimum number of subnets Vnet1 must contain?
questions.explanation:
A NAT gateway is associated with a subnet and takes precedence over instance-level public IP addresses for new outbound connections. Therefore, associating it with Subnet2 would prevent VM2 from using its own public IP address for outbound access. Subnet1 cannot use the NAT gateway because it contains VM1 with a Basic SKU public IP, and NAT Gateway is unsupported with subnets containing Basic resources. A NAT gateway also cannot be deployed to GatewaySubnet. A new subnet is consequently required in addition to Subnet1, Subnet2, and GatewaySubnet, for a total of four subnets.

**Learn more:** [What is Azure NAT Gateway?](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/nat-gateway/nat-overview) · [Manage a public IP address with a NAT gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/ip-services/configure-public-ip-nat-gateway)

You have an Azure subscription containing an ExpressRoute Standard gateway named GW1.  
  
You need to upgrade GW1 to support ExpressRoute FastPath. The solution must minimize downtime.  
  
Which SKU should you use?
questions.explanation:
ExpressRoute FastPath is supported by the Ultra Performance and ErGw3AZ gateway SKUs. A Standard gateway can be upgraded to Ultra Performance within the non-availability-zone SKU family without deleting and recreating the gateway. Switching from a non-availability-zone SKU to ErGw3AZ requires a migration or recreation and can interrupt connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Azure ExpressRoute FastPath: Features, availability, and limitations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/about-fastpath) · [Configure a virtual network gateway for ExpressRoute using the Azure portal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/expressroute-howto-add-gateway-portal-resource-manager)

You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure virtual WAN named VWAN1 and a virtual network named VNet1. VWAN1 is connected to the on-premises networks and VNet1 in a full-mesh topology. The virtual hub routing preference for VWAN1 is **AS Path**.  
  
You need to route traffic from VNet1 to `10.61.1.5`.  
  
Which path will be used?
questions.explanation:
`10.61.1.5` is within the `10.61.0.0/16` prefix advertised by each branch. With an AS Path hub-routing preference, Azure Virtual WAN prefers the route with the shortest BGP AS-path irrespective of whether the advertisement was learned through VPN or ExpressRoute. The Branch3 ExpressRoute advertisement has no AS-path prepends, so it is the preferred route.

**Learn more:** [Virtual WAN virtual hub routing preference - Azure Virtual WAN](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-wan/about-virtual-hub-routing-preference)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Application Gateway for a web app named App1. The application gateway supports end-to-end encryption.  
  
You configure the HTTPS listener by uploading an enterprise-signed certificate.  
  
You need to ensure that the application gateway can deliver end-to-end encryption for App1. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the Unhealthy threshold setting in the custom probe.
Enable the SSL profile to the listener.
Set Listener type to Multi site.
Upload the public key certificate to the HTTP settings.

questions.explanation:
End-to-end TLS requires encrypted client-to-gateway traffic and a separate TLS connection from Application Gateway to the backend. The backend server certificate must be trusted by Application Gateway; uploading its public key certificate to the HTTP settings allows that backend TLS connection and completes end-to-end encryption.

**Learn more:** [Configure end-to-end TLS by using Application Gateway with the portal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/end-to-end-ssl-portal) · [Enabling end-to-end TLS on Azure Application Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/ssl-overview)

![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783807279953-os795w9t.png)  
  
You need to ensure that every app can access resources in a virtual network named VNet1 without sending traffic through the internet.  
  
How many integration subnets should you create?
questions.explanation:
Azure App Service virtual network integration lets multiple apps in the same App Service plan use the same integration subnet. Therefore, the two apps in ASP1 share one subnet, while ASP2 and ASP3 each need an integration subnet, totaling three. Multi-plan subnet join is a separate capability with additional same-subscription and subnet-sizing requirements that are not established here.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains these resources:  
  
- A virtual network named Vnet1  
- Two subnets named subnet1 and AzureFirewallSubnet  
- A public Azure Firewall named FW1  
- A route table named RT1 associated with Subnet1  
- A route in RT1 that sends `0.0.0.0/0` to FW1  
  
After deploying 10 servers running Windows Server to Subnet1, you find that none of the virtual machines has activated.  
  
You need to ensure that the virtual machines can activate.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Add an internet route to RT1 for the Azure Key Management Service (KMS).
On FW1, create an outbound service tag rule for Azure Cloud.
On FW1, configure a DNAT rule for TCP port 1688.

questions.explanation:
Azure Windows VMs use the Azure Key Management Service (KMS) endpoint for activation on TCP port 1688. When a user-defined default route directs all traffic through a firewall, KMS activation traffic requires an Internet route exception so it can reach the KMS service. Microsoft documents exempting KMS traffic with a route that sends it directly to the Internet in forced-tunneling scenarios.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot Azure Windows virtual machine activation problems](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-machines/windows/troubleshoot-activation-problems)

questions.question:
You have an Azure Front Door instance named FD that includes an origin group named OG1.  
  
You need to configure a health probe for OG1. The solution must minimize the traffic generated by the health probe.  
  
Which HTTP method should you use?
questions.explanation:
Azure Front Door supports GET and HEAD health probes. HEAD obtains the response status and headers without returning a response body, so it produces less traffic and is the recommended method for reducing load and cost on origins.\
\
**Learn more:** [Health probes - Azure Front Door](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/frontdoor/health-probes) · [Best Practices - Azure Front Door](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/frontdoor/best-practices)

questions.question:
You have an Azure Front Door instance named FD that includes an origin group named OG1.  
  
You need to configure a health probe for OG1. The solution must minimize the traffic generated by the health probe.  
  
Which HTTP method should you use?
questions.explanation:
An Azure App Service private endpoint provides private connectivity through Azure Private Link, eliminating public internet exposure when public network access is disabled. Azure Front Door Premium can connect to an App Service origin by using Private Link, and public direct access to the app is disabled after the private endpoint is enabled.

**Learn more:** [Connect Azure Front Door Premium to an App Service origin with Private Link](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/frontdoor/standard-premium/how-to-enable-private-link-web-app) · [Use private endpoints for Azure App Service apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/overview-private-endpoint)

questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription.  
  
You intend to deploy Azure Firewall Premium, enable every Premium feature, and configure both network and application rules.  
  
Which rule type will the firewall process first?
questions.explanation:
When threat intelligence-based filtering is enabled, Azure Firewall gives its threat-intelligence rules the highest priority and processes them before network and application rules. Infrastructure rules are evaluated only later when applicable configured rules do not match.\
\
**Learn more:** [Configure Azure Firewall rules | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/rule-processing)

questions.domain: Design and implement Azure network security services
questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription.  
  
You intend to deploy Azure Firewall Premium, enable every Premium feature, and configure both network and application rules.  
  
Which rule type will the firewall process first?

options.text: Change the port on the listener

questions.explanation:
An Azure Application Gateway health probe can test the backend service on port 8080. If that probe fails, the affected backend server is marked unhealthy and Application Gateway stops sending it traffic, routing requests to the other healthy server in the backend pool instead.

**Learn more:** [Health monitoring overview for Azure Application Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/application-gateway-probe-overview) · [Backend health for Azure Application Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/application-gateway-backend-health)

questions.question:
You have an Azure virtual network named VNet1 that includes the subnets shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783841175276-rzplfuvn.png)  
  
You need to deploy an Azure Application Gateway named AppGW1 to VNet1.  
  
Where can AppGW1 be deployed?
questions.explanation:
Azure Application Gateway requires its own dedicated subnet, and that subnet cannot contain virtual machines or other resource types. Subnet2 has no connected resources, whereas Subnet1 contains virtual machines and GatewaySubnet is reserved for VPN gateways.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Application Gateway infrastructure configuration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/configuration-infrastructure)

questions.domain: Design and implement application delivery services
questions.question:
Solution: You reset the gateway for Vnet1.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
Windows Point-to-Site VPN clients must download and install an updated VPN client package after virtual network peering or another network-topology change, so they receive the new route to the peered virtual network. Resetting the VPN gateway does not provide that route to the client.\
\
**Learn more:** [About Point-to-Site VPN routing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/vpn-gateway-about-point-to-site-routing) · [Create, change, or delete Azure virtual network peering](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-manage-peering)

questions.domain: Design, implement, and manage connectivity services
questions.question:
Solution: You resize the gateway in Vnet1 to a higher SKU.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
Azure P2S clients can access a peered virtual network when the gateway VNet enables gateway transit and the peer uses the remote gateway. Windows VPN clients must download and install a new VPN client package after a topology change so that they receive routes for the peered VNet. Increasing the VPN gateway SKU affects gateway capacity and performance, not the required client route configuration.\
\
**Learn more:** [Configure VPN gateway transit for virtual network peering](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/vpn-gateway-peering-gateway-transit) · [About Point-to-Site VPN routing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/vpn-gateway-about-point-to-site-routing)

questions.domain: Design, implement, and manage connectivity services
questions.question:
Solution: You resize the gateway in Vnet1 to a higher SKU.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
P2S VPN clients only receive routes that were included in the VPN client configuration package generated at the time of setup or last download. When gateway transit is enabled after the peering is configured, the routes to the peered VNet's address space are not automatically pushed to already-connected P2S clients. To fix this, the VPN client configuration package must be regenerated and reinstalled on the client so it obtains the routes to the newly reachable peered network. Enabling BGP on the Vnet1 gateway does not update the P2S client's route table with the Vnet2 address space, so it does not resolve the reported connectivity issue.

**Learn more:** [Configure VPN gateway transit for virtual network peering - Azure VPN Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/vpn-gateway-peering-gateway-transit) · [About Point-to-Site VPN routing - Azure VPN Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/vpn-gateway-about-point-to-site-routing)

questions.domain: Design, implement, and manage connectivity services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Solution: You download and reinstall the VPN client configuration package on Client1.  
  
Does this solution meet the goal of ensuring that Client1 can communicate with Vnet2?
questions.explanation:
When VNet peering is configured with gateway transit, point-to-site clients that were connected before the peering was established do not automatically receive routing information for the newly reachable peered virtual network. To make the peered VNet's address space known to the client, the VPN client configuration package must be downloaded again from the virtual network gateway and reinstalled on the client. This refreshes the routes distributed to the client, allowing traffic to Vnet2 to be routed correctly through the P2S VPN tunnel, since Vnet1 already allows gateway transit and Vnet2 is configured to use the remote gateway.

**Learn more:** [Azure VPN Gateway FAQ | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/vpn-gateway-vpn-faq) · [P2S VPN Cannot Connect To Peered Virtual Network Which Uses Another Virtual Networks Gateway - Microsoft Q&A](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/1294150/p2s-vpn-cannot-connect-to-peered-virtual-network-w)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription containing the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783828563139-1ieeojys.png)  
  
Gateway1 provides access to App1 through the URL `https://app1.contoso.com`.  
  
You create a new web app named App2.  
  
You need to configure Gateway1 to provide access to App2 through the URL `https://app2.contoso.com`. The solution must minimize administrative effort.  
  
What should you configure on Gateway1?

options.text: a backend pool and a routing rule
a listener and a routing rule
a listener, a backend pool, and a routing rule
a listener and a backend pool

questions.explanation:
An Application Gateway routes traffic received by a listener according to its request-routing rule, which specifies the target backend pool. App2 therefore needs a backend pool, a listener for `app2.contoso.com`, and a routing rule connecting them. The existing `*.contoso.com` certificate can be reused for the HTTPS listener because it covers `app2.contoso.com`.

**Learn more:** [Hosting multiple sites on Azure Application Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/multiple-site-overview) · [Azure Application Gateway request routing rules configuration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/configuration-request-routing-rules)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an on-premises network.  
  
You have an Azure subscription containing a virtual network named VNet1 and a private Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster named AKS1. VNet1 connects to your on-premises environment through an Azure ExpressRoute circuit. AKS1 connects to VNet1.  
  
You need to deploy an off-cluster ingress controller for AKS1. The solution must enable connectivity from the on-premises environment to containerized workloads hosted on AKS1.  
  
Which Azure service should you use?
questions.explanation:
Azure Application Gateway, integrated with AKS through the Application Gateway Ingress Controller (AGIC) add-on, provides an off-cluster Layer 7 ingress solution. It can expose AKS workloads through a private frontend in the virtual network, which on-premises clients can reach over ExpressRoute.

**Learn more:** [Network topology and connectivity for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/scenarios/app-platform/aks/network-topology-and-connectivity) · [What is Application Gateway Ingress Controller?](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/ingress-controller-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that includes a user named Admin1 and a resource group named RG1.  
  
RG1 includes an Azure Network Watcher instance named NW1.  
  
You need to ensure that Admin1 can apply a lock to NW1. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.  
  
Which role should you assign to Admin1?
questions.explanation:
Creating a management lock requires the `Microsoft.Authorization/locks/write` permission. Of the available roles, User Access Administrator grants Microsoft.Authorization management permissions that include this operation; assigning it at the NW1 resource scope limits its scope in accordance with least privilege.

**Learn more:** [Azure permissions for Management and governance - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/permissions/management-and-governance) · [Azure built-in roles for Management and governance - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles/management-and-governance)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) policy in prevention mode that is associated with an Azure Front Door instance.  
  
You need to configure the policy to meet the following requirements:  
  
- Log all connections from Australia.  
- Deny all connections from New Zealand.  
- Deny all further connections from the network 131.107.100.0/24 if there are more than 100 connections during a one-minute period.  
  
What is the minimum number of objects you should create?

options.text: three custom rules that each has one condition
one custom rule that has three conditions
one custom rule that has one condition
one rule that has two conditions and another rule that has one condition

questions.explanation:
Each requirement demands a different action (Log, Block, or rate-limited Block) and, in the case of the rate limit requirement, a different rule type (rate limit rule vs. match rule). Because an Azure Front Door WAF custom rule applies a single action to all of its (AND-combined) match conditions, the three distinct outcomes cannot be produced by one rule or by mixing conditions within a rule. The solution therefore requires three separate custom rules — one match rule with a geo-match condition for Australia set to Log, one match rule with a geo-match condition for New Zealand set to Block, and one rate limit rule with an IP-match condition for 131.107.100.0/24 and a threshold of 100 requests per minute set to Block — each rule containing exactly one condition.

**Learn more:** [WAF Custom Rule for Azure Front Door | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/web-application-firewall/afds/waf-front-door-custom-rules) · [Configure a rate limit rule for Azure Front Door WAF](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/web-application-firewall/afds/waf-front-door-rate-limit-configure)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription containing these resources:  
  
- A virtual network named Vnet1  
- Two subnets named subnet1 and AzureFirewallSubnet  
- A public Azure Firewall named FW1  
- A route table named RT1 associated with Subnet1  
- A rule in RT1 that routes `0.0.0.0/0` to FW1  
  
After you deploy 10 servers running Windows Server to Subnet1, you find that none of the virtual machine operating systems have been activated.  
  
You need to make sure that the virtual machines can be activated.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: On FW1, create an outbound network rule that allows traffic to the Azure Key Management Service (KMS).
To Subnet1, associate a network security group (NSG) that allows outbound access to port 1688.
Deploy an Azure Standard Load Balancer that has an outbound NAT rule.

questions.explanation:
Azure Windows virtual machines use the Azure Key Management Service (KMS) endpoint for activation, over port 1688. Because the default route sends all outbound traffic through FW1, Azure Firewall must have an outbound network rule that permits traffic to the Azure KMS service.

**Learn more:** [Windows VM activation no longer works in Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-machines/windows/windows-activation-stopped-working) · [Troubleshoot Azure Windows virtual machine activation problems](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-machines/windows/troubleshoot-activation-problems)

questions.domain: Design and implement Azure network security services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure virtual network containing a subnet named Subnet1. Subnet1 is associated with a network security group (NSG) named NSG1. NSG1 blocks all outbound traffic unless it is explicitly allowed.  
  
Subnet1 contains virtual machines that need to communicate with the Azure Cosmos DB service.  
  
You need to create an outbound security rule in NSG1 that allows the virtual machines to connect to Azure Cosmos DB.  
  
What should you include in the solution?
questions.explanation:
Azure NSG rules support service tags as a destination, and the `AzureCosmosDB` service tag represents Azure Cosmos DB for outbound rules. Using that tag in an allow rule permits the required outbound traffic without maintaining individual service IP prefixes.

**Learn more:** [Azure service tags overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/service-tags-overview) · [Security considerations for Azure Cosmos DB](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/security-considerations)

questions.domain: Design and implement Azure network security services
questions.question:
You are planning IP addressing for subnets in Azure virtual networks.  
  
Which resource type requires IP addresses within the subnets?
questions.explanation:
An internal load balancer requires a private frontend IP address from the selected virtual-network subnet. This frontend address is the internal endpoint through which clients reach the load-balanced service.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer portal settings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/manage) · [Azure Load Balancer components](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/components)

questions.domain: Design and implement Azure network security services
questions.question:
You are planning IP addressing for subnets in Azure virtual networks.  
  
Which resource type requires IP addresses within the subnets?
questions.explanation:
An Azure Firewall must be deployed into a virtual network that is in both the same region and the same resource group as the firewall. The Azure Firewall FAQ states explicitly: the Azure Firewall and virtual network must be in the same resource group (only the public IP may be in a different RG), and the firewall does not store or serve data outside its region. AF1 is created in RG1 in West US, so the target VNet must be RG1 + West US. Only Vnet1 (RG1, West US) satisfies both — Vnet4 is West US but in RG2, and Vnet2 is in RG1 but in Central US. The answer is Vnet1 only (C).

**Learn more:** [Azure Firewall FAQ](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/firewall-faq)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an on-premises network.  
  
You have an Azure subscription that includes a virtual network.  
  
You have an ExpressRoute service provider.  
  
You plan to connect the Azure virtual network to the on-premises network by using an ExpressRoute circuit.  
  
You create a new ExpressRoute circuit.  
  
You need to provision the new circuit.  
  
Which information must you provide to the service provider?
questions.explanation:
An ExpressRoute circuit is uniquely identified by its service key (s-key). The customer provides this key to the connectivity provider so that the provider can provision the circuit.

**Learn more:** [Azure ExpressRoute: Circuit configuration workflow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/expressroute-workflows) · [Azure ExpressRoute: circuits and peering](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/expressroute-circuit-peerings)

questions.domain: Design and implement Azure network security services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must connect Vnet2 and Vnet3. The solution must satisfy the virtual networking and business requirements.  
  
Which two actions should be included in the solution? Each correct answer represents part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: On the peering from Vnet1, select Allow gateway transit.
On the peerings from Vnet2 and Vnet3, select Use remote gateways.
On the peerings from Vnet2 and Vnet3, select Allow gateway transit.
On the peering from Vnet1, select Use remote gateways.
On the peering from Vnet1, select Allow forwarded traffic.

questions.explanation:
Azure gateway transit requires **Allow gateway transit** on the gateway-hosting hub VNet’s peering and **Use remote gateways** on each spoke VNet’s peering. This lets Vnet2 and Vnet3 use the gateway in Vnet1. A spoke can use only one remote gateway, and the remote gateway must be configured to allow gateway transit.

**Learn more:** [Hub-and-spoke network topology - Azure Virtual Network](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/design-guide/hub-spoke) · [Azure virtual network peering CLI reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/network/vnet/peering?view=azure-cli-latest)

questions.domain: Design and implement core networking infrastructure
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an internal Basic Azure Load Balancer named LB1 with two frontend IP addresses. LB1's backend pool contains two Azure virtual machines named VM1 and VM2.  
  
You need to configure the LB1 rules as shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783826710395-yf7ronqi.png)  
  
What should you configure for each rule?
questions.explanation:
When multiple Azure Load Balancer frontend IP configurations route TCP traffic to the same backend pool on the same backend port, Floating IP must be enabled on every applicable load-balancing rule. This preserves the frontend destination address for the backend VMs so they can distinguish traffic for each frontend and return it correctly. Session persistence is unrelated to permitting reuse of the backend port.

**Learn more:** [Multiple frontends for Azure Load Balancer](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/load-balancer-multivip-overview) · [Azure Load Balancer Floating IP configuration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/load-balancer-floating-ip)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains a virtual network named VNet1 and the resources listed in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783884311350-f00hcf4n.png)  
  
You need to implement a solution for traffic that originates from VNet1. The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
- Perform transparent proxying to external web servers.  
- Inspect all outbound TLS traffic.  
- Minimize costs.  
  
Which resource should you include in the solution?
questions.explanation:
Azure Firewall operates as a transparent proxy by default when outbound traffic is routed through it. Azure Firewall Premium supports outbound TLS inspection, whereas Azure Firewall Standard does not. FW1 is an existing Azure Firewall Premium deployment in VNet1, so it satisfies the outbound proxying and TLS-inspection requirements without the cost of deploying another qualifying resource. [Azure Firewall explicit proxy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/explicit-proxy) [Azure Firewall features by SKU](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/features-by-sku)

**Learn more:** [Azure Firewall explicit proxy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/explicit-proxy) · [Azure Firewall features by SKU](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/firewall/features-by-sku)

questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription.  
  
You plan to deploy an app named App1 that users will access by using Azure Application Gateway.  
  
You need to deploy the application gateway for App1.  
  
What should you create first?

options.text: an Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) policy

questions.explanation:
Azure Application Gateway requires a dedicated subnet in a virtual network for its deployment. A managed identity, X.509 certificate, and WAF policy can be configured only when needed for particular gateway features or workloads.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Application Gateway infrastructure configuration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/configuration-infrastructure)

questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription containing the public IP addresses shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783795670230-w1wm0gp3.png)  
  
You plan to deploy a NAT gateway named NAT1.  
  
Which public IP addresses can be used as NAT1's public IP address?
questions.explanation:
A Standard Azure NAT gateway can use Standard SKU IPv4 public IP addresses; it cannot use Basic SKU public IP addresses or IPv6 public IP addresses. IP3 is the only address with a Standard SKU, IPv4, and static allocation.\
\
**Learn more:** [Manage a public IP address with a NAT gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/ip-services/configure-public-ip-nat-gateway) · [Troubleshoot Azure NAT Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/nat-gateway/troubleshoot-nat)

questions.domain: Design and implement Azure network security services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription containing a resource group named RG1 and a virtual network named VNet1.  
  
You need to deploy Azure Firewall to RG1 while minimizing administrative effort.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: Create a secured virtual hub named AzureFirewallHub.
Create a new virtual network named AzureFirewallNetwork.
Create a new resource group named AzurFirewellRescurceGroup.
On VNet1, create virtual subnet named AzureFirewallSubnet

questions.explanation:
Azure Firewall requires a dedicated subnet named `AzureFirewallSubnet` in the virtual network where it is deployed. Because VNet1 already exists, creating that subnet in VNet1 avoids creating unnecessary resource groups, virtual networks, or a Virtual WAN secured hub.

**Learn more:** [Azure Firewall and traffic inspection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/design-guide/azure-firewall) · [Azure virtual networks and subnets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/design-guide/vnets-subnets)

questions.domain: Design and implement private access to Azure services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an on-premises datacenter named DC1 that contains two routers.  
  
You have an Azure subscription. The subscription includes a virtual network named VNet1 and a zone-redundant ExpressRoute virtual network gateway named GW1 that uses the ErGw3Az SKU. GW1 is connected to VNet1.  
  
DC1 connects to VNet1 by using an ExpressRoute Standard circuit named Circuit1. The DC1 routers are configured as the endpoints for Circuit1. Circuit1 traffic crosses two physical links.  
  
During a link outage, the connection requires three minutes to fail over.  
  
You need to ensure that failovers between the links occur in less than one second.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: On the routers, configure Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD).
For GW1, change SKU to UltraPerformance.
For GW1, set Active-active mode to Enabled.

questions.explanation:
BFD provides low-overhead, subsecond detection of a link failure between the ExpressRoute Microsoft Enterprise Edge devices and the customer or partner edge routers. Configuring BFD on the routers avoids waiting for the typical BGP keepalive and hold timers, which can otherwise take up to three minutes to detect a failed link.

**Learn more:** [Configure BFD over ExpressRoute](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/expressroute-bfd)

You plan to publish a website that will use the FQDN `www.contoso.com`. The website will be hosted using the Azure App Service apps shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783810356021-xhjyed9y.png)  
  
You plan to use Azure Traffic Manager to manage traffic routing for `www.contoso.com` between AS1 and AS2. You create a Traffic Manager profile named TMprofile1, which uses the weighted traffic-routing method.  
  
You need to ensure that Traffic Manager routes traffic for `www.contoso.com`.  
  
Which DNS record should you create?

options.text: two A records that map www.contoso.com to 131.107.100.1 and 131.107.200.1
a CNAME record that maps www.contoso.com to TMprofile1.azurefd.net
a CNAME record that maps www.contoso.com to TMprofile1.trafficmanager.net
a TXT record that contains a string of as1.contoso.com and as2.contoso.com in the details

questions.explanation:
